searchText: given the tx pool design that geth has settled on (which I understand is more tolerant) - will we see similar chaos / variance? https://twitter.com/barnabemonnot/status/1364096261331120130?s=20 https://twitter.com/barnabemonnot/status/1364096265861042176?s=20 i think it's still a fairly pathological case, though yes the main reason it happens in the first place is that there is a "backlog" of similarly priced transaction (equal-ish max fees) waiting to be included. but the alternative of having very strict transaction pools is possibly worse for UX see also our discussion on the latest peep an EIP! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AC1FS3LmoT4 haha i'm halfway through it now 😄 I could see blocks being <50% full but then spiking to 100% when basefee drops below specific round-number thresholds (e.g. 10 gwei) due to the backlog of txs. While this is chaotic from a block usage standpoint, it's much better than a less-tolerant alternative from a UX perspective I think that the oscillator pattern won't play out IRL for the following reason: If the basefee drops to the "crowded level", the next block will become full. Actors will be able to predict that with a lead time of 14s. Similarly, the following block will have the max 1.125x price, predictably. The ability to foresee this will allow some parties to use that to their advantage, which mitigates the effect. That mitigation is a dampening process (the downward oscillation amplitude is reduced) because the block will now contain the transactions of these active agents. The heuristic I am using is induced behaviour change to some minor percentage of participants. Those who use the forecast to modify their fee stand to gain a lot for little cost, and the system benefits from the dampening effect of their action I developed this idea when playing gidget-gadget. At every saw tooth I would think: "I could sneak a transaction in right now because the next block is going to balloon and then be empty, ready for mine to be included at marginally higher fee" Which corresponds to a situation where there are: - zero happy to pay to play users - many stingy users all camped at one level - a minority of slightly less stingy active users who, if they act rationally, will get included and "smooth the sawtooth" correct, this is a good reason too. though in my mind the most probable scenario is 1. lots of people join to transact at the same time, their wallets set their max-fees to the same value 2. basefee shoots up until it prices everyone out 3. every time basefee lowers to under that backlog of fixed max-fees users it shoots up again (there are lots of people to include!) but indeed in that case the "empty block" part of the sawtooth need not be empty if more users join the system, but there could still be this flip flop because of the backlog Interesting. That's a good point - if 5000 users all use the same wallet at the same time, their fee prediction is the same. (BFx2) But what if the wallet added some noise to the prediction? The level would be less crisp, and less likely to create instability The round number problem is only a problem if wallets are asking humans to set the various per-gas costs. UIs should generally *not* be doing this for 1559 transactions. By "prediction" I just mean "the fee" So the 5000 users all submit their txs, and their fees are e.g. normally distributed quick question on the ropsten implementation for 1559 which activates in <2d... A.) was the same 12.5MM gas limit applied to this testnet as mainnet (I believe it is currently set at 8MM) . B.) are there parties that are planning to hit the network with surge traffic to replicate mainnet? appreciated.. See: https://discord.com/channels/595666850260713488/745077610685661265/855485146177863722 for question B. The gas limit doesn't change with London, it is still miner voted. So whatever London's gas limit is right now, that will become the gas target with London. That's not 100% true 👆, the number that miners vote on will need to be 2x'ed at the fork block, or blocks will start "shrinking", see "As a Ropsten miner or Goerli/Rinkeby validator, what do I need to do?" here: https://blog.ethereum.org/2021/06/18/london-testnets-announcement/ Hmm, I thought we decided against that? I am probably mis-remembering. Yeah, client teams thought it was simpler to just get people to 2x the limit. Only thing that kind of sucks is that there doesn't seem a way to specify in advance "target this gas limit when block X hits"

excerpts.author: ankur2534
excerpts.content: I could see blocks being <50% full but then spiking to 100% when basefee drops below specific round-number thresholds (e.g. 10 gwei) due to the backlog of txs. While this is chaotic from a block usage standpoint, it's much better than a less-tolerant alternative from a UX perspective

excerpts.author: perama
excerpts.content:
I think that the oscillator pattern won't play out IRL for the following reason:

If the basefee drops to the "crowded level", the next block will become full. Actors will be able to predict that with a lead time of 14s. 

Similarly, the following block will have the max 1.125x price, predictably. The ability to foresee this will allow some parties to use that to their advantage, which mitigates the effect. 

That mitigation is a dampening process (the downward oscillation amplitude is reduced) because the block will now contain the transactions of these active agents. 

The heuristic I am using is induced behaviour change to some minor percentage of participants. Those who use the forecast to modify their fee stand to gain a lot for little cost, and the system benefits from the dampening effect of their action

excerpts.author: perama
excerpts.content: I developed this idea when playing gidget-gadget. At every saw tooth I would think: "I could sneak a transaction in right now because the next block is going to balloon and then be empty, ready for mine to be included at marginally higher fee"

excerpts.author: perama
excerpts.content:
Which corresponds to a situation where there are:
- zero happy to pay to play users
- many stingy users all camped at one level
- a minority of slightly less stingy active users who, if they act rationally, will get included and "smooth the sawtooth"

excerpts.author: barnabemonnot
excerpts.content:
correct, this is a good reason too. though in my mind the most probable scenario is 1. lots of people join to transact at the same time, their wallets set their max-fees to the same value 2. basefee shoots up until it prices everyone out 3. every time basefee lowers to under that backlog of fixed max-fees users it shoots up again (there are lots of people to include!)

but indeed in that case the "empty block" part of the sawtooth need not be empty if more users join the system, but there could still be this flip flop because of the backlog

excerpts.author: perama
excerpts.content:
Interesting. 

That's a good point - if 5000 users all use the same wallet at the same time, their fee prediction is the same. (BFx2)

But what if the wallet added some noise to the prediction?

The level would be less crisp, and less likely to create instability

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: The round number problem is only a problem if wallets are asking humans to set the various per-gas costs.  UIs should generally *not* be doing this for 1559 transactions.

excerpts.author: perama
excerpts.content:
By "prediction" I just mean "the fee"

So the 5000 users all submit their txs, and their fees are e.g. normally distributed
